title: The Corps of Discovery Votes on Winter Camp
text:
By late November 1805 the Lewis and Clark expedition had reached the mouth of the Columbia River, after a year and a half of travel from St. Louis. Rain fell almost without pause, their clothes were rotting, and they had to decide where to spend the winter before starting home in spring.

The captains could simply have given an order. Instead, on 24 November, they put the question to the whole party. William Clark wrote down each person's choice in his journal: whether to stay on the north side of the river, cross to the south side and look for a site, or go back upstream.

Two names on that list stand out. York, Clark's enslaved servant, voted with the rest, at a time when he would have had no vote anywhere in the United States. Sacagawea, the Shoshone woman traveling with her husband and infant son, was also asked. Clark recorded her view under the nickname "Janey": she favored a place where there were plenty of "Potas", the wapato roots the party relied on for food.

Most of the party wanted to cross to the south side and examine the country there. They did, and in December they built Fort Clatsop near present-day Astoria, Oregon. They spent a hard, wet winter there and set out for home in March 1806.
lesson: Asking everyone, including those usually left out, makes a hard decision a shared one. People endure a tough plan better when they had a voice in choosing it.
people: Meriwether Lewis, William Clark, York, Sacagawea
location: Mouth of the Columbia River, Washington and Oregon, USA
source: The Journals of the Lewis and Clark Expedition, William Clark's entry for 24 November 1805 (ed. Gary Moulton)
